Udayanīyā
------------------------------------------
A सोमयाग has an introductory or opening rite called प्रायणीया and a closing rite called उदयनीया.
These sacrifices belong to the इष्टि type (see IṢṬI for details.)
The प्रायणीया is performed after the दीक्षा (consecration of the sacrificer) day. Going out to fetch the सोम creepers is the most important part of this rite. Offering of चरु (porridge-like preparation) and आज्य (ghee) to some deities is also done.
In the उदयनीया इष्टि, the concluding rite is performed in the fire of the shed called prācīnavaṁśa, erected with bamboos, with four oblations.

udarabandha
(‘belly-band’)
------------------------------------------
Iconographical works describe kaṭi-बन्ध (waist-band) and उदरबन्ध (belly-band) for certain images like those of गणेश.
It is of various forms and is to be shown above the navel and below the chest, covering the belly.

Udāsīs
------------------------------------------
The उदासीस् are an ascetic sect of the Sikhs founded by Śrīcand (A.
-1629), the elder son of गुरु Nānak (A.

-1539). The word udāsī is derived from the Sanskrit word udāsin, which means one who is indifferent towards the comforts and attachments of the world.
Śrīcand was a devoted Sikh and a saintly person. His object in establishing the order of the उदासीस् was to propagate the mission of his ड़थेर्. Though he was not anointed as the next गुरु by his ड़थेर्, he kept an amicable relationship with all the Gurus.
Bābā Gurudittā, the eldest son of गुरु Hargobind (A.

-1644), was sent by the गुरु to assist and to succeed Śrīcand.
Bābā Gurudittā appointed four head-preachers: Almast; Phūl; Goind (or Gonda); Bālū Husnā. They were given his own dress—which became the peculiar Udāsī uniform—as also the dhuni (smouldering embers) from Śrīcand’s dhuni. These four established four new seats of the Udāsī sect.
The उदासीस् proved to be zealous preachers of सिखिस्म् and carried its message to all the corners of the country and beyond. They revered and recited the bāṇī (sayings) of the Gurus, but retained their separate identity. They took control of the Sikh places of worship and protected them when needed.
The उदासीस् recruit their followers from all castes and professions. In their monasteries it is the Guru Granthasāhib that is recited. They do not subscribe to the Sikh rites and use the bell, conch and gong in religious services.
They wear white or ochre or red clothes. There is also one group that goes naked. Having matted hair and smearing the body with ashes are also common.
They have built buṅgas (resthouses) around the Harmandir complex in Amritsar. These are also prominent centres of learning, आयुर्वेद being one of the important subjects taught.
The most important centres of this sect in North India are: the Brahm Būṭā Akhāḍā and Saṅgalānvālā Akhāḍā at Amritsar; Nirañjaniyā Akhāḍā at Patiala (both in Punjab); Pañcaitī Akhāḍā at Hardwar (in Uttar Pradesh).

Udaṅka
------------------------------------------
A sage often mentioned in the Mahābhārata, उदङ्क had propitiated विष्णु through his तपस् and had got some boons.
Once Kṛṣṇa—after the कुरुक्षेत्र war—came to his hermitage to pay his respects. Thinking that the war which had decimated many क्षत्त्रिय warriors, had been manoeuvred by him, the sage tried to curse him. However, he soon realised (by the cosmic form exhibited by कृष्ण) his mistake and sought boons from him.
Udaṅka—also known as Uttaṅka—was a disciple of the sage गौतम. While bidding goodbye to him after completing his studentship, गौतम asked him to get the ear-rings of Madayantī, the queen of the king Saudāsa, for his wife अहल्या. उदङ्क got them after a great effort.
